hero.title: Business Cards & Spend Management Index
hero.subtitle: How six platforms explain spending controls, rewards and cross-border business payments.
hero.lede: Compare what six platforms publish about their products, and explore my analysis of their messaging, Instagram content and application entry screens.
hero.draft_note: Draft for editorial review. This edition is not published.

findings.dek: The three findings with the strongest support across the six. Each starts from what the sources say, names the customer question it raises, gives my reading, and links to the analysis and the test that follow from it.

items.question: Is the advertised reward what I would earn?
items.title: Reward rates and their conditions were often stated in different places
items.body: Five of the six platforms published a reward rate. At two, visible statements on different pages did not agree for some plans: Venn's cards page says its cashback has no tiers, thresholds or caps, while its pricing footnote says cashback is earned only on the first $5,000 of card spend a month on Essentials and the first $25,000 on Plus; Loop's cards page says rewards come on all spend, while its earn-rate table lists USD, EUR and GBP spend as not eligible on the Basic plan. Airwallex's visible pages say 1%; a 2% figure appears only in the page's title metadata. Float and Keep publish their conditions on the pricing page.
items.denominator: 5 platforms that published a reward rate. For Ramp, a Canadian rewards rate was not found in the reviewed sources.
items.reading: A reader who meets the rate on one page and its condition on another has to connect the two to know what they would earn.
items.short_title: You sometimes need two pages to understand the reward
items.summary: Venn and Loop published reward statements that did not agree for some plans. A business owner needs the rate and its conditions together to understand which spending qualifies.
items.figure_label: platforms that published a reward rate

items.question: Does "no FX fee" mean I never pay to convert?
items.title: Every "no FX fee" claim described one kind of transaction
items.body: All six platforms published a statement of no FX fee, no FX markup or a 0% FX fee. Each covered a specific case, such as spending from a balance in the same currency, four approved currencies or a USD card, and each site or its terms describes a fee, rate or margin for other conversions: for example an automatic conversion fee in Airwallex's card terms, and a note on Ramp's global page that conversions stay subject to exchange rates and fees. Keep's pricing page lists an FX fee of 0% for banking, while its card agreement sets a 3% card conversion fee.
items.denominator: 6 of 6 platforms; card spending, FX conversion and transfers were checked separately for each.
items.reading: A general "no FX fee" line answers the question only for the case it covers; the other cases are priced on other pages or in the terms.
items.short_title: “No FX fee” doesn’t cover every transaction
items.summary: All six platforms used a no-FX-fee claim for a specific situation. What you pay can depend on the currency, the balance you hold and the transaction.
items.figure_label: platforms limited the no-FX-fee claim to a specific situation

items.question: Can I tell whether I qualify, and what happens after I start?
items.title: Few first screens said who can apply or what happens next
items.body: I followed each platform's main start button to its first screen in a browser. Loop's sign-up was the only one that listed the steps ahead and what they need (CRA ID, date of birth, government ID). Ramp states its eligibility rules (entity, Business Number, Canadian bank account) on its card page, but its sign-up screen asks only for an email. Venn's sign-up says there is no personal credit check, while its Quebec exclusion appears elsewhere on the site. Float's demo form and Airwallex's sign-up ask for contact details without saying what follows, and Keep's start buttons lead to a closed-applications page.
items.denominator: 6 of 6 first screens observed in a browser on 23 October 2026; none was followed past the first screen.
items.reading: At most first screens, whether you qualify and what follows was on another page or not stated before the next step. This is a reading of six first screens, not of how many people start or finish an application.
items.short_title: Most first screens didn’t explain what happens next
items.summary: Only Loop’s first screen listed the steps ahead. The six routes served different purposes, including account sign-ups, a card application and a demo request. Keep’s self-serve application route was closed when checked.
items.figure_label: first screens listed the steps ahead

findings.take: Open your main offer page and follow its button. Can a new customer understand the conditions and what happens next without searching elsewhere?

compare.note: A row is not a quote. Peoples Trust Company issues four of the six cards (Venn, Ramp, Keep, Airwallex); how each card is funded or repaid differs, as the first column of Cards, rewards & costs shows. This edition does not compare FX costs: a fair comparison would need the same currencies, amount, timing, plan and fees. The eligibility column covers applying from Canada only; availability in other countries is not assessed, and worldwide figures in the proof are labelled as worldwide where the source says so.
compare.unclear: Where a label says what could not be confirmed, two published statements did not settle the point (reconciliation class D in the 23 October 2026 research). For Airwallex, a follow-up check on 30 October 2026 found that pricing lists up to 1% cash rebates on local CAD spend and links to promotion terms whose period ends on 31 December 2025 unless Airwallex notifies otherwise; no extension was found, so current eligibility needs confirmation. The card page still states 1% cashback with no cap, and a 2% figure seen in the page metadata on 23 October stays in the evidence. Pricing also lists a credit line for corporate cards without explaining its eligibility or repayment terms.
compare.pricing_note: Prices are in Canadian dollars unless stated otherwise. Per-user charges, annual billing and additional platform fees are shown where applicable.
compare.currency_note: Fees cover different transactions and conditions. These figures are not a like-for-like cost comparison.

examples.dek: Four observed examples of how an offer, proof or next step was explained. They are examples to learn from, not winning platforms.

items.title: A savings figure labelled as the provider's own estimate
items.body: The Bells of Steel case study presents $10,000 a year in savings and says in the text that Loop calculated it. The same site's homepage averages ($40,000 a year and 12 hours a week) carry no basis I could find, so the labelled figure stands out.
items.lesson: A reader can weigh a number when they know who calculated it and how.

items.title: "Up to" with the threshold in a numbered footnote
items.body: Float's pages say "Up to 1% cashback". The pricing page footnote gives the condition: 1% applies above $25k of monthly spending per card program. The rate below that threshold was not on the pages I reviewed.
items.lesson: "Up to" signals a condition; the footnote states it, but only on the pricing page.

items.title: Eligibility stated on the card page
items.body: Ramp's Canadian card page lists what a business needs: a Canadian, US or UK-registered entity, a Business Number and a linked Canadian bank account, underwritten on the business with no personal guarantee. The sign-up screen itself asks for one email and does not repeat the list.
items.lesson: A reader can check whether they qualify before giving an email, if they read the card page first.

items.title: A competitor named inside a customer story
items.body: Airwallex's Adaria Vending Services story, about a Canadian company expanding into the US, names Venn and Wise as tools the company used before. The outcomes it reports are qualitative, such as cards issued in under 24 hours.
items.lesson: Naming the prior setup makes the switch concrete; the outcome is still the provider's account of its customer.

venn.offer: 1% cashback, no FX fee from matching-currency balances, and plans from $0. The cards page says the cashback has no caps; the pricing footnote says it is earned only on the first $5,000 of card spend a month on Essentials and the first $25,000 on Plus.
venn.proof: The visible homepage counts agree at 15,000+ (a 4,000+ figure is in the page code but set not to display). The Flow case study reports time saved without figures. The transfers page claims FX rates up to 2.75% cheaper than banks, with no basis I could find.
venn.observation: The cashback statement on the cards page and the footnote on pricing cannot both be read literally for Essentials and Plus customers.
missing: Steps after account creation (needs an account)
venn.take: Your cards page and your pricing page are read as one offer. Ask your team whether a visitor who sees only your highest-traffic page would know which spend earns the reward on each plan.
venn.audience: Canadian businesses: "business banking built for Canada". The site says Venn is not available to businesses in Quebec.
venn.problem: Cost against the banks: the transfers page says "FX rates up to 2.75% cheaper than the banks".
venn.benefit: Accounts, corporate cards with 1% cashback, free local transfers and low FX.

question.text: Will I earn 1% on all my card spend?
question.detail: The cards page says the cashback has no caps; the pricing footnote limits the eligible spend on Essentials and Plus. Both are published and they disagree.

float.offer: Up to 1% cashback, 0.25% FX, USD cards without foreign transaction fees, account interest of 2.5% (up to 3.5% in a promotion) and credit up to $3M+ subject to eligibility. The 1% applies above $25k of monthly spending per card program (pricing footnote); the 3.5% is a 12-month promotion on new balances above a baseline (promotion terms).
float.proof: The Impact Kitchen story reports more than 100 hours a year saved. "Save up to 90% on FX" carries no basis I could find.
float.observation: Both "up to" figures, cashback and interest, lead with the best case; the condition for each is on another page (a pricing footnote and the promotion terms).
missing: What happens after a demo is booked
float.take: An "up to" figure invites the question "up to, if what?". A practical test: put the condition for each "up to" figure on the same screen as the figure, and measure qualified demo requests against questions about rates.
float.audience: Canadian businesses: "Built in Canada, for Canada."
float.problem: Manual finance work: the product menu calls expense management "The end of manual expense work."
float.benefit: Business accounts, corporate cards, payments and spend management from one provider.

question.text: What do I earn below $25k a month of card spend?
question.detail: The pricing footnote says 1% applies above $25k a month per card program; the rate below that threshold was not on the pages I reviewed.

ramp.offer: Free and Plus plans, CAD and USD cards, and CAD or USD spend without the FX markup; the global page says conversions stay subject to applicable exchange rates and fees. A Canadian rewards rate was not found in the reviewed sources.
ramp.proof: 85,000 customers worldwide, a receipt figure labelled as internal data, and quotes from large brands. None of the proof is specific to Canada.
ramp.observation: The Canadian pages pair Canadian eligibility rules with worldwide proof (85,000 customers) and a header demo link that leaves the Canadian site.
missing: Card model and repayment terms (Canada Card Supplement, capture request R2)
Ramp's Rewards Terms (Canadian schedule), capture request R1
Steps after the email (needs an application)
ramp.take: When a regional page borrows global proof and links, the buyer has to work out which parts apply to them. Ask your team to mark every claim on your regional page as local or global, and test labelling global figures as such.
ramp.audience: Canadian businesses ("Canada, meet Ramp."), with eligibility open to Canadian, US or UK-registered entities.
ramp.problem: Controlling spend in advance: a homepage section is headed "Control spend before it happens."
ramp.benefit: Cards, expenses and bill payments for Canadian businesses.

question.detail: The cards page lists the entity, Business Number and bank account required; the sign-up screen asks for an email and does not repeat the list.

loop.offer: No FX fee in four currencies, points on card spend, free payments for now, and credit up to $1M. A 1.5% fee applies to card purchases in other currencies, and on the Basic plan the earn-rate table lists USD, EUR and GBP spend as not eligible for points.
loop.proof: The Bells of Steel case study labels its $10,000 saving as Loop's calculation. The homepage averages ($40,000 a year and 12 hours a week) and the "first" claim carry no basis I could find.
loop.observation: The same site shows both a labelled estimate and unlabelled averages, which makes the difference easy to see.
missing: Steps after the first form (needs a submission)
loop.take: Where your proof states its basis, a buyer can weigh it; where it does not, they have to trust it. Ask your team which three figures on your homepage could be challenged, and add the source line to each.
loop.audience: Canadian businesses that work across borders: "Global Banking for Canadian Businesses".
loop.problem: Bank fees on foreign currency: a homepage section is headed "Loop vs The Banks", and the card is called "Canada's first no-FX credit card".
loop.benefit: FX-free credit cards, free international transfers and global accounts.

question.text: What happens after I open an account?
question.detail: A panel on the sign-up screen lists the two steps that follow and what they need: business information (CRA ID, structure, website) and identity (date of birth, government ID).

keep.offer: Points with up to 56 fee-free days, multi-currency accounts in five currencies, and 90-day trials on plans from $79 a month. The card agreement sets a 3% card conversion fee that I did not find on the card, pricing or FAQ pages.
keep.proof: "Trusted by 5,000+ Canadian Companies" and "Canada's #1", with no basis for the ranking on the pages I reviewed. No case study was found.
keep.observation: The marketing pages still present the offer, start buttons and "Applications do not impact your credit score", while the one sign-up route they lead to says applications are closed.
missing: Whether the closed sign-up route affects every Keep product
keep.take: If a journey is paused, the pages that send people to it are the first thing they see. Ask your team what a visitor who clicks your main button today actually reaches, and whether the page they leave from says so.
keep.audience: Any business, in the headline ("All-in-one banking for any business"); the site also says 5,000+ Canadian companies use it.
keep.problem: Limits and manual expenses: the card is promised with "higher limits" and "expenses that do themselves".
keep.benefit: A business card with higher limits, automated expenses and capital to grow.

question.detail: The marketing pages show start buttons and "Applications do not impact your credit score"; the self-serve sign-up route they lead to says new applications are closed. The message names no product.

airwallex.offer: 1% cashback on card spend, no foreign transaction fee from a held currency, transfers with $0 fees on local rails, and plans from $0.
airwallex.proof: The homepage gives 200,000 and 600,000+ businesses; the 600,000 figure says it includes customers served through platforms. The Adaria story is Canadian and reports qualitative outcomes.
airwallex.observation: The page title says 2% cashback while every visible statement says 1%. Search engines and link previews may use page titles and social metadata, so a figure there can reach buyers who never see the page.
missing: The automatic conversion fee level for card purchases
airwallex.take: Page titles and social metadata can travel further than the page itself. Ask your team whether every title and preview description on your site states the same offer as the page it leads to.
airwallex.audience: "Global businesses", with a homepage section on gaining "a competitive edge in the Canadian market".
airwallex.problem: Running finance across countries: the homepage covers payments, treasury and spend for businesses operating locally and globally.
airwallex.benefit: Payments, treasury and spend managed in one platform.

question.detail: Every visible statement says 1%; the 2% figure appears only in the page's title metadata, and the rebate terms were not found.

patterns.dek: Patterns that hold across the group, with the platforms that support them and the exceptions. None shows cause and effect.

items.title: Figures often appeared without their basis
items.body: Every platform published a customer count or savings figure. Savings and ranking claims without a stated basis appeared at Venn (FX up to 2.75% cheaper than banks), Float (save up to 90% on FX), Loop (average savings) and Keep ("Canada's #1").
items.exceptions: Loop's case study labels its estimate; Ramp labels its receipt figure as internal data; Airwallex says its 600,000 figure includes customers served through platforms.
items.denominator: 6 of 6 published such a figure; 4 of 6 gave at least one without a basis I could find.

items.title: Spend controls were described alike; the plan behind each feature was not
items.body: All six describe card controls and receipt matching, and five describe approval workflows; Keep's card page instead says you set the rules once rather than approving purchases one at a time. Every platform names QuickBooks. At Float, Ramp and Airwallex the larger accounting systems (NetSuite, Sage Intacct, Microsoft Dynamics 365 Business Central) sit on higher plans, which the pricing pages show but the feature pages mostly do not.
items.exceptions: Loop does not say which kinds of limit its controls set. Airwallex's pricing page lists each integration under its plan; Venn and Loop name only QuickBooks and Xero.
items.denominator: 6 of 6 platforms, from their spend-management, card and pricing pages.

patterns.take: Buyers of financial products look for the basis behind a number and for the plan that includes the feature they need. Ask your team which figure on your site a careful buyer would question first, and whether each feature page says which plan includes it.

tests.dek: Three tests a marketing team could run on its own pages, each tied to a finding above and laid out in the same chain: observed evidence, customer question, my interpretation, hypothesis, measurement. They are proposals to discuss, not results, and none needs a provider's internal data.

items.title: Put the reward condition beside the rate
items.observation: Venn's cards page says its cashback has no tiers, thresholds or caps, while its pricing footnote limits the eligible card spend on Essentials and Plus. Loop's cards page says rewards come on all spend, while its earn-rate table lists USD, EUR and GBP spend as not eligible on Basic.
items.question: Will I earn the advertised rate on my plan and at my spend level?
items.reading: When the rate and its condition sit on different pages, a reader of either page sees only part of the offer.
items.hypothesis: With the condition beside the rate, readers can check it before applying, so the version with the condition will produce at least as many qualified applications per card-page visitor, with fewer rewards questions from new customers.
items.change: Show the cap, threshold or plan condition in the same block as the headline rate on the card page.
items.comparable: The rate, the terms, the design and the button stay the same. Split card-page traffic at random, with the same traffic sources, the same attribution window and the same definition of a qualified application in both versions.
items.measure: Qualified applications (meeting your eligibility rules) per visitor to the card page. Count button clicks separately.
items.guardrail: Rewards questions to sales and support in the first 30 days after sign-up, and plan mix.
items.limitation: Inconclusive if rewards are not a main reason buyers choose you, if traffic is too small to separate the two versions, or if pricing or rewards change during the test. Legal review of the wording comes first.

items.title: Say which transactions a "no FX fee" claim covers
items.observation: All six platforms published a no-FX-fee statement that covered a specific case, such as a matching-currency balance, four currencies or a USD card, and each site or its terms prices other conversions elsewhere. Keep's pricing page lists an FX fee of 0% for banking while its card agreement sets a 3% card conversion fee.
items.question: Will I pay to convert when I buy in a currency I do not hold?
items.reading: A general line answers that question only for the case it covers; the reader has to find the other cases in pricing or the terms.
items.hypothesis: A line that names the covered transaction, followed by one line on what applies otherwise, will produce at least as many completed applications from the FX or cards page, with fewer FX questions and disputed charges after sign-up.
items.change: Replace a general "no FX fees" line with one that names the case it covers, followed by one line saying what applies otherwise.
items.comparable: The page layout, offer, fees, terms and button stay the same. Split traffic at random with the same audiences and attribution window; if traffic is low, run the versions in matched consecutive periods and record the dates.
items.measure: Completed applications from the FX or cards page.
items.guardrail: FX-related support questions and disputed charges in the first 60 days after sign-up.
items.limitation: Inconclusive if seasonal travel or trade cycles swamp the difference, or if fees change during the test. Required disclosures stay in place; this changes the summary, not the terms.

items.title: State eligibility and the next step before the form
items.observation: Loop's sign-up lists the two steps ahead and what they need. Ramp's eligibility rules sit on its cards page rather than its sign-up screen. The Venn, Float and Airwallex first screens asked for contact or account details without saying what follows, and Keep's route was closed.
items.question: Do I qualify, and what happens after I give my details?
items.reading: At most first screens the answer to either question was on another page or not stated before the next step.
items.hypothesis: A short "Before you start" list above the first field will raise the share of form starts that become qualified applications, without reducing the number of qualified applications.
items.change: Add a short "Before you start" list above the first form field: who can apply, what you need, which provinces are served, and what happens after submitting.
items.comparable: The form fields, verification steps, traffic sources and the definition of a qualified application stay the same. Split traffic at random with consistent audiences.
items.measure: The share of form starts that become qualified applications. Report clicks, form starts, submissions and qualified applications as separate numbers.
items.guardrail: Total form starts and completed submissions from eligible businesses, so the list does not turn away people who qualify.
items.limitation: Inconclusive if eligibility rules change during the test or most traffic is already qualified. Never remove necessary identity or eligibility checks.

method.scope: An independent comparative marketing case study of how six selected platforms explain business cards, spend management and cross-border payments to Canadian businesses. It reads dated public sources and the first screen of each application journey. It does not test product performance, assess regulatory compliance or recommend a provider for your business.
method.selection: The founder selected these six platforms as a comparison set of providers that market business cards and spend management to Canadian businesses. They are not presented as the largest, the most used or the best, and other providers exist.
method.dates: Public pages were fetched by a server on 23 October 2026 from 10:39 a.m. to 10:48 a.m. Toronto time, a browser pass checked them from 12:00 p.m. to 12:14 p.m., and two more pages were fetched later the same day: the Airwallex fee schedule at 2:10 p.m. and the Float Payments page at 2:33 p.m. Every observation carries its own capture time.
method.public_only: I read only public pages: no accounts, logins, forms submitted, credit checks or transactions. A server fetch does not run JavaScript, so a browser pass then checked what visitors see, followed each enquiry journey to its first screen and looked up the FINTRAC and Bank of Canada registries. Where the two differed, the page reports what a visitor sees and keeps the server reading in the evidence.
statuses: An applicable official source states it. This does not mean it was tested.
The pages I reviewed did not establish it. It may exist elsewhere.
Relevant sources differ and the difference is unresolved.
An applicable source says it is not available.
limitations: Pages change. Every observation is dated to its capture and may no longer be current.
The browser pass used a normal Chrome profile that was not signed in to any of the six providers. Journeys were followed only to the first screen; nothing was submitted.
US and global pages were not used as Canadian facts. Where a Canadian page carried US disclosures, that is recorded as an observation about the page.

Regulatory statements and registry entries (FINTRAC and the Bank of Canada, checked on 23 October 2026) are recorded in each platform's evidence as supporting detail. They are not a compliance assessment, an endorsement or a safety rating.
This edition does not compare FX costs or product performance and does not recommend a provider.
method.corrections: If an observation is wrong or out of date, email Hello@helpmemarketing.com with the page and the correction. Confirmed corrections will be made with a dated note.
corrections_log: Loop's homepage time saving. Before this correction, the Bells of Steel example said "$40,000 and 12 hours a year", and observation O-LOP-12 and the downloadable observations CSV said "$40,000 and 12 hours saved a year"; Loop's proof line gave no unit. The homepage states "Businesses save an average of $40,000 annually and 12 hours weekly". Corrected in the Bells of Steel example, Loop's proof line, observation O-LOP-12 and the CSV.

help.heading: If you market a financial product
help.body: I can read your own messaging and application journey the way this case study reads these six: how the offer, its conditions, the proof and the next step come across to a buyer. This is a free review of your marketing by Help Me Marketing. It is not advice on which card or platform to choose, and it is not financial, legal or regulatory advice.

overview.title: Overview
overview.dek: I reviewed six platforms’ websites to see how they explain their offers and what happens when someone clicks to apply. These three things stood out.
overview.about_intro: This page serves two kinds of reader. If you are comparing card and spend platforms, it sets out what six providers publish, each fact linked to its source. If you market a product, it is my independent case study of how they explain it: the offer, the proof and the path to applying. None of the six is a client, and I have no view of their internal strategy or results.
overview.heading: What stood out

compare.title: Compare products
compare.dek: Compare what each platform publishes about its cards, rewards, fees and spending tools.

messaging.title: Messaging & offers
messaging.dek: For each platform: who the pages speak to, the problem they emphasise, the benefit they promise, the offer and its conditions, the proof they supply, and one customer question the pages answer or leave open.

journeys.title: Application journeys
journeys.dek: What happens when a Canadian business clicks each provider's main start button, observed in a browser up to the first screen. Nothing was submitted, no account was created and no application was tested past that screen.

lessons.title: Lessons & tests
lessons.dek: Patterns across the six, and three tests a marketing team could run on its own pages. Each test follows the same chain as the rest of the page.

venn.asks: Google or Microsoft sign-in, or email, password and password confirmation
venn.elig: "No personal credit check or guarantee"; no eligibility list
venn.next: "Get started in 5 minutes"; the steps after the account is created are not described
venn.limit: None on this screen; elsewhere the site says Venn is not available in Quebec

float.asks: Eight questions marked required, a referral code marked optional, "How did you hear about us" (required status not recorded); a reCAPTCHA check
float.next: Consent to be contacted; nothing on what happens after booking

ramp.elig: Not on this screen; the cards page lists entity, Business Number and Canadian bank account
ramp.next: The heading "Apply for Ramp's corporate card"; no later steps listed

loop.asks: Full name, legal business name, email, mobile phone (or Google sign-up)
loop.elig: None beyond the information each step asks for
loop.next: A panel lists the next two steps: business information (CRA ID, structure, website) and identity (date of birth, government ID)
loop.limit: None on this screen; elsewhere the card is said not to be available to Quebec sole proprietors

keep.start: Homepage, card page and pricing: every start button found
keep.asks: Nothing; log-in is offered to existing customers
keep.next: "We're not accepting new applications at this time"; no product named
keep.limit: The self-serve sign-up route was closed to new applicants when checked

airwallex.next: Continuing agrees to receive marketing communications; no later steps listed
airwallex.limit: None on this screen; elsewhere card use is said not to be for Quebec sole proprietors

journeys.note: Observed in a browser on 23 October 2026 between 12:09 p.m. and 12:12 p.m. Toronto time (Keep at 12:02 p.m.), from a normal Chrome profile not signed in to any provider. Each journey was followed to its first screen only: no form was submitted, no account was created and no application was tested past that screen. A progress indicator or time estimate was not used to judge journey length. Ramp's header "See a demo" link leads to a page outside the Canadian site.
journeys.reading: Loop's sign-up was the only first screen that described what comes next. At the other five, a prospective customer would find eligibility, if at all, on another page (Ramp's cards page, Venn's Quebec note) or not before the next step, and Keep's route was closed. This reads six first screens; it says nothing about how many people start, abandon or finish an application.
journeys.test: Test 3 under Lessons & tests turns this into a proposal: state who can apply and what happens next above the first form field, and measure the share of form starts that become qualified applications.

legend: Tables, platform facts and evidence lists. Each fact links to the page it came from and its capture time; a status label marks anything that is not a plain published fact.
My interpretation, kept apart from the sources: findings, readings and patterns. A reading can be wrong even where the sources are right.
What this means for your marketing team
A short lesson drawn from a section's evidence, with one question or test and the measure to watch.
An experiment a team could run on its own pages, with a hypothesis and a measure. None has been run.
about: What six providers publish about their business cards, cross-border payments and spend tools, and how their pages and first application screens explain them.

I selected them as a comparison set: each markets business cards or spend management to Canadian businesses. It is a selected cohort, not the six largest or best, and not a complete survey of the market.

Product facts come from Canadian pages or terms that apply to Canadian businesses. Three of the six state Quebec exclusions (Venn for all Quebec businesses, Loop and Airwallex for Quebec sole proprietors). Ramp's customer count is worldwide, and Airwallex's figures do not say whether they are global or Canadian; both are labelled that way.
What it can and cannot establish

It can establish what a public page said at a recorded time, and where two statements differ. It cannot establish how the products perform, what customers understand or do, how well any provider's marketing works, why a provider wrote what it did, or whether anything complies with regulation.

chain.note: Every conclusion on this page follows that order. From public pages I do not infer a provider's intent, what customers understood, any effect on conversions, revenue or acquisition efficiency, paid distribution, or non-compliance, and I give no baselines or uplift figures.
